## The Problem

Fabricated citations in academic papers have grown sharply since the widespread adoption of generative AI writing tools. A Lancet audit of 2.5 million biomedical papers found hallucinated reference rates rising 12-fold between 2023 and early 2026 [@topaz2026fabricated]. GPTZero's audit of NeurIPS 2025 found over 100 confirmed hallucinated citations across 53 accepted papers despite rigorous peer review [@gptzero2026neurips]. Separate estimates project roughly 147,000 hallucinated citations across arXiv, bioRxiv, SSRN, and PMC in 2025 alone [@zhao2026llmhallucinationswildlargescale].

Existing peer review and editorial safeguards largely fail to catch these errors before publication. The problem spans disciplines: biomedical research, AI/ML conferences, legal filings, and government reports.

While AI use is driving a surge in publications [see @wheeler2026llmbook for a practical overview], the same large language models that create this problem can also be used to verify citations at scale. VerusCite ([veruscite.com](https://veruscite.com)) is a tool to automatically extract and verify citations from uploaded documents. This report documents the accuracy of the V1 verification pipeline against a hand-labeled ground truth corpus.

## Approach

### Design Philosophy

Even in documents with hallucinated citations, the majority of references are legitimate. A tool with a high false positive rate -- flagging real papers as hallucinations -- would waste a reviewer's time chasing false alarms rather than finding actual problems. VerusCite prioritizes **precision over recall**: it is better to miss some hallucinations than to incorrectly flag verified citations.

The target false positive rate for hallucination flags is below 1%. Recall for detecting actual hallucinations is around 70-80%. This tradeoff means a human reviewer spends most of their time on citations that genuinely need attention rather than dismissing false reports.

The application is designed for human-in-the-loop review. Each citation's verification status can be manually overridden, and the interface surfaces the reasoning behind each determination so reviewers can make informed decisions quickly.

### Comparison to Similar Tools

This approach is similar to Pangram, which also emphasizes low false positive rates for AI-generated content detection. Their published materials discuss the same tradeoff: when base rates of problematic content are low, even small false positive rates cause most flagged items to be false alarms [@emi2024falsepositives].

## Pipeline Architecture

VerusCite processes documents in two stages:

1. **Citation Extraction** -- An LLM reads the document text and identifies individual references, parsing out structured fields (title, authors, year, journal, DOI).
2. **Citation Verification** -- Each extracted citation is checked against external sources to determine whether it exists as described.

### Verification Categories

The checker assigns each citation one of four statuses:

| Status | Meaning |
|--------|---------|
| **Verified** | Citation confirmed to exist via CrossRef or web search |
| **Minor Error** | Citation likely exists but has metadata discrepancies (wrong year, volume, pages) |
| **Hallucination** | No evidence the cited work exists as described |
| **Not Found** | Unable to confirm or deny -- includes bare URL citations and paywalled/very recent works with insufficient search results |

### Verification Method

Verification proceeds in two passes:

1. **Static CrossRef lookup** -- A title/DOI search against CrossRef metadata. Fast and free. Confirms roughly 60% of legitimate citations without needing web search.
2. **Web search verification** -- Citations not resolved by CrossRef are sent to a web-search-enabled LLM (Perplexity or OpenAI web search tools) to locate evidence of the publication.

The primary checker configurations reported here are **Perplexity** (hosting Gemini 3.1 Flash Lite and OpenAI GPT-5.4-nano), **direct Google Gemini 3.5 Flash Lite**, and **OpenAI** direct (`gpt-5.4-nano` and `gpt-5.6-luna`, with web search). Having multiple providers is important operationally -- any single provider experiences periodic outages or rate limits. Results reported here represent the range across these configurations.

Cost is kept low by using smaller models with web search rather than large frontier models. A full corpus check (36 papers, ~2,288 citations) runs between roughly **$0.35–$0.65 per paper** depending on the model.

## Ground Truth

```{python}
#| output: false
totals = ground_truth_totals()
n_citations = int(totals.sum())
n_verified = int(totals.get("verified", 0))
n_hallucination = int(totals.get("hallucination", 0))
n_minor = int(totals.get("minor_error", 0))
n_not_found = int(totals.get("not_found", 0))
```

The V1 validation corpus contains **`{python} n_citations`** hand-labeled citations across **36 documents**. Sources are intentionally heterogeneous:

- Papers with known hallucinations identified by others on social media (Chris Carothers, David Buil-Gil)
- GPTZero's NeurIPS 2025 audit [@gptzero2026neurips]
- Papers flagged by Reviewer3 [@reviewer3]
- A ChatGPT deep-research output where all 12 citations are fabricated
- Clean papers (dissertation excerpts, open-access criminology, PLoS ONE articles)
- MDPI and preprint samples

Of the `{python} n_citations` citations, `{python} n_verified` (`{python} f"{100*n_verified/n_citations:.1f}"`%) are verified, `{python} n_minor` (`{python} f"{100*n_minor/n_citations:.1f}"`%) have minor errors, `{python} n_hallucination` (`{python} f"{100*n_hallucination/n_citations:.1f}"`%) are hallucinations, and `{python} n_not_found` (`{python} f"{100*n_not_found/n_citations:.1f}"`%) are not found. The corpus skews heavily toward verified citations (as real documents do), which makes false positive rate the critical metric.

## Extraction Results

Citation extraction uses an LLM to parse the document text and identify individual references. The table below shows extraction accuracy **and wall-clock speed** against the ground truth (latest kept runs, **2026-07-30**).

```{python}
#| label: tbl-extraction
#| tbl-cap: "Extraction accuracy and speed by model (pypdfium2 OCR)"
md_table(extraction_table())
```

```{python}
#| output: false
ext = extraction_report(V1)
ext_sorted = ext.sort_values("correctly_extracted", ascending=False).reset_index(drop=True)
default_row = ext[ext["model"] == "gemini-3.1-flash-lite"].iloc[0]
nano_rows = ext[ext["model"] == "gpt-5.4-nano"]
nano_row = nano_rows.iloc[0] if len(nano_rows) else None
default_rate = 100.0 * float(default_row["correctly_extracted"]) / float(default_row["real_citations"])
default_wall_min = float(default_row["wall_elapsed_seconds"]) / 60.0
_dpm = default_row["docs_per_minute"]
default_dpm = float(_dpm) if pd.notna(_dpm) else float("nan")
nano_wall_min = float(nano_row["wall_elapsed_seconds"]) / 60.0 if nano_row is not None else float("nan")
speedup = (nano_wall_min / default_wall_min) if (nano_row is not None and default_wall_min > 0) else float("nan")
```

Extraction is very accurate across models. **Gemini 3.1 Flash Lite is the default production extraction model**: it correctly extracts about **`{python} f"{default_rate:.2f}"`%** of citations (matching `gpt-5.4-nano` on correct count, with fewer extras) and finishes the full 36-document corpus in about **`{python} f"{default_wall_min:.1f}"` minutes** wall time (~`{python} f"{default_dpm:.1f}"` docs/min), roughly **`{python} f"{speedup:.1f}"`×** as fast as `gpt-5.4-nano` on the same batch. Cost remains on the order of a few cents per paper for the full corpus.

The few "extra" rows that remain are typically table fragments or rare non-bibliography lines the model still surfaces; numbered discursive footnotes and author bios are filtered in the current pipeline. PDF text extraction uses `pypdfium2`, with link-annotation DOI repair so LaTeX rule-drawn underscores in DOIs are recovered from hyperlink targets when the selectable text layer has spaces.

`gpt-5.4-nano` and `gpt-5.6-luna` are retained as OpenAI comparison baselines (luna is slightly cheaper and faster wall-clock than nano here, with a few more missing/extra citations).

## Checker Results

```{python}
#| label: tbl-checking
#| tbl-cap: "Checker accuracy by model/provider"
md_table(checking_table())
```

```{python}
#| output: false
chk = checking_report(V1)
# Parse percentage strings like "0.4% (7)" / "69.5% (98/141)"
def _pct(series):
    return series.astype(str).str.extract(r"([\d.]+)%", expand=False).astype(float)

fp_hall_max = float(_pct(chk["verified_fp_hallucination"]).max())
nv_recall_min = float(_pct(chk["not_verified_recall"]).min())
nv_recall_max = float(_pct(chk["not_verified_recall"]).max())
hall_recall_max = float(_pct(chk["hallucination_recall"]).max())
best_hall_idx = _pct(chk["hallucination_recall"]).idxmax()
best_hall_model = str(chk.loc[best_hall_idx, "model"])
best_hall_provider = str(chk.loc[best_hall_idx, "provider"])
crossref_med = int(chk["verified_via_crossref"].median())
cost_min = float(chk["cost_usd"].min())
cost_max = float(chk["cost_usd"].max())
cost_per_min = cost_min / 36.0
cost_per_max = cost_max / 36.0
cheapest_idx = chk["cost_usd"].idxmin()
cheapest_model = str(chk.loc[cheapest_idx, "model"])
cheapest_provider = str(chk.loc[cheapest_idx, "provider"])
```

Key metrics:

- **FP → Hallucination**: Percentage of actually-verified citations incorrectly flagged as hallucinations. All configurations stay at or below **`{python} f"{fp_hall_max:.1f}"`%**.
- **Not-Verified Recall**: Percentage of actual problems (hallucinations + minor errors + not-found) correctly identified. Ranges from about **`{python} f"{nv_recall_min:.0f}"`–`{python} f"{nv_recall_max:.0f}"`%** across the kept runs.
- **Hallucination Recall**: Percentage of actual hallucinations correctly flagged. The best configuration here (**`{python} best_hall_model`** via **`{python} best_hall_provider`**) achieves about **`{python} f"{hall_recall_max:.1f}"`%**.

### Cost Breakdown

```{python}
#| label: tbl-cost
#| tbl-cap: "Cost breakdown per full-corpus checker run (36 papers)"
costs = cost_comparison_table()
costs["Per Paper (USD)"] = (costs["Total (USD)"] / 36).round(2)
md_table(costs)
```

Full-corpus checker cost ranges from about **$`{python} f"{cost_min:.2f}"`–$`{python} f"{cost_max:.2f}"`** (~$`{python} f"{cost_per_min:.2f}"`–$`{python} f"{cost_per_max:.2f}"` per paper). The cheapest kept configuration is **`{python} cheapest_model`** (`{python} cheapest_provider`) at ~$`{python} f"{cost_per_min:.2f}"` per paper. Perplexity-hosted Gemini 3.1 Flash Lite sits in the middle on cost while offering strong not-verified and hallucination recall; OpenAI `gpt-5.6-luna` improves hallucination recall versus `gpt-5.4-nano` at a similar verified false-positive rate and mid-range cost; OpenAI `gpt-5.4-nano` remains the most expensive kept run (more web searches) with strong not-verified recall.

### CrossRef as First Pass

Across the kept checker runs, about **`{python} crossref_med`** citations are confirmed via static CrossRef lookup alone (no web search needed) -- on the order of two-thirds of verified citations -- which keeps per-citation expenses low and latency down.

## Privacy

VerusCite uses only zero data retention (ZDR) models from all providers. Uploaded documents are not used for model training by any third party.

Additionally, the pipeline minimizes what is sent to external LLMs. Citation extraction uses text search on the locally-extracted PDF text first -- only the citation strings themselves are sent to an LLM for structured parsing. During verification, only the parsed citation metadata (title, authors, year) is sent to web search, not the full document text. The full PDF content never leaves the server.

## Limitations and Next Steps

The V1 corpus is heterogeneous by design, but 36 documents is a limited sample. The next evaluation (V2) will use the same prompts and pipeline but a **completely different validation set** -- different documents, different domains, different sources of known hallucinations. This ensures the system is not overtrained on the particular examples in V1.

Known limitations of the current evaluation:

- Ground truth labels for some documents were seeded from the checker itself and hand-reviewed, which may introduce subtle bias toward the checker's own patterns.
- "Not found" is an inherently ambiguous category -- some citations are bare URLs, others exist but are difficult to locate via web search (paywalled, very recent, or in non-English databases).
- The corpus over-represents arXiv preprints relative to other domains (law, humanities, clinical medicine).

## Reproducibility

All data for this report is public at [github.com/apwheele/veruscite-data](https://github.com/apwheele/veruscite-data). The `V1/` directory contains:

- `ground_truth.csv` -- hand-labeled citations with `expected_status`
- `extraction_run/` -- raw extraction outputs per model (kept: Gemini 3.1 Flash Lite, gpt-5.4-nano, gpt-5.6-luna, **2026-07-30**)
- `checking_run/` -- raw checker outputs per model (Perplexity Gemini 3.1 Flash Lite, Perplexity openai/gpt-5.4-nano, direct Gemini 3.5 Flash Lite, OpenAI gpt-5.4-nano, OpenAI gpt-5.6-luna)
- `manifest.json` -- run IDs used in this report (`default_extraction_model`: `gemini-3.1-flash-lite`)
